readings.c1s2:
of this primary parallelogram, any point, <math>z'</math>, of the plane being, as it is called, ''congruent'' to a definite point, <math>z</math>, of the primary parallelogram, <math>z'-z</math> being of the form <math>m\omega+m'\omega'</math>, where <math>m</math>, <math>m'</math> are integers. Such a function cannot be an integral function, since then, if, in the primary parallelogram <math>|f(z)|<\text{M}</math>, it would also be the case, on a circle of centre the origin and radius <math>\text{R}</math>, that <math>|f(z)|<\text{M}</math>, and therefore, if <math>\Sigma a_nz^n</math> be the expansion of the function, which is valid for an integral function for all finite values of <math>z</math>, we should have <math>|a_n|<\text{MR}^{-n}</math>, which can be made arbitrarily small by taking <math>\text{R}</math> large enough. The function must then have singularities for finite values of <math>z</math>.

We consider only functions for which these are poles. Of these there cannot be an infinite number in the primary parallelogram, since then those of these poles which are sufficiently near to one of the necessarily existing limiting points of the poles would be arbitrarily near to one another, contrary to the character of a pole. Supposing the constant <math>c</math> used in naming the corners of the parallelograms so chosen that no pole falls on the perimeter of a parallelogram, it is clear that the integral <math>\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int f(z)dz</math> round the perimeter of the primary parallelogram vanishes; for the elements of the integral corresponding to two such opposite perimeter points as <math>z</math>, <math>z+\omega</math> (or as <math>z</math>, <math>z+\omega'</math>) are mutually destructive. This integral is, however, equal to the sum of the residues of <math>f(z)</math> at the poles interior to the parallelogram. Which sum is therefore zero. There cannot therefore be such a function having only one pole of the first order in any parallelogram; we shall see that there can be such a function with two poles only in any parallelogram, each of the first order, with residues whose sum is zero, and that there can be such a function with one pole of the second order, having an expansion near this pole of the form <math>(z-a)^{-2}+</math>(power series in <math>z-a</math>).

Considering next the function <math>\phi(z)=[f(z)]^{-1}\frac{df(z)}{dz}</math>, it is easily seen
readings.c1s3:
that an ordinary point of <math>f(z)</math> is an ordinary point of <math>\phi(z)</math>, that a zero of order <math>m</math> for <math>f(z)</math> in the neighbourhood of which <math>f(z)</math> has a form, <math>(z-a)^m</math> multiplied by a power series, is a pole of <math>\phi(z)</math> of residue <math>m</math>, and that a pole of <math>f(z)</math> of order <math>n</math> is a pole of <math>\phi(z)</math> of residue <math>-n</math>; manifestly <math>\phi(z)</math> has the two periods of <math>f(z)</math>. We thus infer, since the sum of the residues of <math>\phi(z)</math> is zero, that for the function <math>f(z)</math>, the sum of the orders of its vanishing at points belonging to one parallelogram, <math>\Sigma m</math>, is equal to the sum of the orders of its poles, <math>\Sigma n</math>; which is briefly expressed by saying that the number of its zeros is equal to the number of its poles. Applying this theorem to the function <math>f(z)-\text{A}</math>, where <math>\text{A}</math> is an arbitrary constant, we have the result, that the function <math>f(z)</math> assumes the value <math>\text{A}</math> in one of the parallelograms as many times as it becomes infinite. Thus, by what is proved above, every conceivable complex value does arise as a value for the doubly periodic function <math>f(z)</math> in any one of its parallelograms, and in fact at least twice. The number of times it arises is called the ''order'' of the function; the result suggests a property of rational functions.

Consider further the integral <math>\int z\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}dz</math>, where <math>f'(z)=\frac{df(z)}{dz}</math>, taken round the perimeter of the primary parallelogram; the contribution to this arising from two opposite perimeter points such as <math>z</math> and <math>z+w</math> is of the form <math>-\omega\int\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}dz</math>, which, as <math>z</math> increases from <math>z_0</math> to <math>z_0+\omega'</math>, gives,
readings.c2s1:
if <math>\lambda</math> denote the generalized logarithm, <math>-\omega\{\lambda[f(z_0+\omega')]-\lambda[f(z_0)]\}</math>, that is, since <math>f(z_0+\omega')=f(z_0)</math>, gives <math>2\pi i\text{N}\omega</math>, where <math>\text{N}</math> is an integer; similarly the result of the integration along the other two opposite sides is of the form <math>2\pi i\text{N}'\omega'</math>, where <math>\text{N}'</math> is an integer. The integral, however, is equal to <math>2\pi i</math> times the sum of the residues of <math>zf'(z)/f(z)</math> at the poles interior to the parallelogram. For a zero, of order <math>m</math>, of <math>f(z)</math> at <math>z=a</math>, the contribution to this sum is <math>2\pi ima</math>, for a pole of order <math>n</math> at <math>z=b</math> the contribution is <math>-2\pi inb</math>; we thus infer that <math>\Sigma ma-\Sigma nb=\text{N}\omega+\text{N}'\omega'</math>; this we express in words by saying that the sum of the values of <math>z</math> where <math>f(z)=0</math> within any parallelogram is equal to the sum of the values of <math>z</math> where <math>f(z)=\infty</math> save for integral multiples of the periods. By considering similarly the function <math>f(z)-\text{A}</math> where <math>\text{A}</math> is an arbitrary constant, we prove that each of these sums is equal to the sum of the values of <math>z</math> where the function takes the value <math>\text{A}</math> in the parallelogram.

We pass now to the construction of a function having two arbitrary periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math> of unreal ratio, which has a single pole of the second order in any one of its parallelograms.
readings.c2s4: of <math>z</math> with <math>\omega</math> and <math>\omega'</math> as periods can be expressed rationally in terms of <math>f(z)</math> and <math>\phi(z)</math>, and that <math>[\phi(z)]^2</math> is of the form <math>4[f(z)]^3+\text{A}f(z)+\text{B}</math>, where <math>\text{A}</math>, <math>\text{B}</math> are constants.

But in fact any complex quantity, <math>\text{P} + i\text{Q}</math>, and in particular any other possible period of the function, is expressible, with <math>\mu</math>, <math>\nu</math> real, in the form <math>\mu\omega + \nu\omega'</math>; for if <math>\omega = \rho + i\sigma</math>, <math>\omega' = \rho' + i\sigma'</math>, this requires only <math>\text{P} = \mu\rho + \nu\rho'</math>, <math>\text{Q} = \mu\sigma + \nu\sigma'</math>, equations which, since <math>\omega'/\omega</math> is not real, always give finite values for <math>\mu</math> and <math>\nu</math>.

In the former case, putting <math>\zeta = 2\pi iz/\Omega</math>, and the function <math>f(z) = \phi(\zeta)</math>, the function <math>\phi(\zeta)</math> has, like <math>\exp(\zeta)</math>, the period <math>2\pi i</math>, and if we take <math>t = \exp(\zeta)</math> or <math>\zeta = \lambda(t)</math> the function is a single valued function of <math>t</math>. If then in particular <math>f(z)</math> is an integral function, regarded as a function of <math>t</math>, it has singularities only for <math>t = 0</math> and <math>t = \infty</math>, and may be expanded in the form <math>\sum_{-\infty}^{\infty} a_n t^n</math>.

Taking the case when the single valued monogenic function has two periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math> whose ratio is not real, we can form a network of parallelograms covering the plane of <math>z</math> whose angular points are the points <math>c + m\omega + m'\omega'</math>, wherein <math>c</math> is some constant and <math>m</math>, <math>m'</math> are all possible positive and negative integers; choosing arbitrarily one of these parallelograms, and calling it the primary parallelogram, all the values of which the function is at all capable occur for points of this primary parallelogram, any point, <math>z'</math>, of the plane being, as it is called, ''congruent'' to a definite point, <math>z</math>, of the primary parallelogram, <math>z'-z</math> being of the form <math>m\omega+m'\omega'</math>, where <math>m</math>, <math>m'</math> are integers. Such a function cannot be an integral function, since then, if, in the primary parallelogram <math>|f(z)|<\text{M}</math>, it would also be the case, on a circle of centre the origin and radius <math>\text{R}</math>, that <math>|f(z)|<\text{M}</math>, and therefore, if <math>\Sigma a_nz^n</math> be the expansion of the function, which is valid for an integral function for all finite values of <math>z</math>, we should have <math>|a_n|<\text{MR}^{-n}</math>, which can be made arbitrarily small by taking <math>\text{R}</math> large enough. The function must then have singularities for finite values of <math>z</math>.

We consider only functions for which these are poles. Of these there cannot be an infinite number in the primary parallelogram, since then those of these poles which are sufficiently near to one of the necessarily existing limiting points of the poles would be arbitrarily near to one another, contrary to the character of a pole. Supposing the constant <math>c</math> used in naming the corners of the parallelograms so chosen that no pole falls on the perimeter of a parallelogram, it is clear that the integral <math>\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int f(z)dz</math> round the perimeter of the primary parallelogram vanishes; for the elements of the integral corresponding to two such opposite perimeter points as <math>z</math>, <math>z+\omega</math> (or as <math>z</math>, <math>z+\omega'</math>) are mutually destructive. This integral is, however, equal to the sum of the residues of <math>f(z)</math> at the poles interior to the parallelogram. Which sum is therefore zero. There cannot therefore be such a function having only one pole of the first order in any parallelogram; we shall see that there can be such a function with two poles only in any parallelogram, each of the first order, with residues whose sum is zero, and that there can be such a function with one pole of the second order, having an expansion near this pole of the form <math>(z-a)^{-2}+</math>(power series in <math>z-a</math>).

Considering next the function <math>\phi(z)=[f(z)]^{-1}\frac{df(z)}{dz}</math>, it is easily seen that an ordinary point of <math>f(z)</math> is an ordinary point of <math>\phi(z)</math>, that a zero of order <math>m</math> for <math>f(z)</math> in the neighbourhood of which <math>f(z)</math> has a form, <math>(z-a)^m</math> multiplied by a power series, is a pole of <math>\phi(z)</math> of residue <math>m</math>, and that a pole of <math>f(z)</math> of order <math>n</math> is a pole of <math>\phi(z)</math> of residue <math>-n</math>; manifestly <math>\phi(z)</math> has the two periods of <math>f(z)</math>. We thus infer, since the sum of the residues of <math>\phi(z)</math> is zero, that for the function <math>f(z)</math>, the sum of the orders of its vanishing at points belonging to one parallelogram, <math>\Sigma m</math>, is equal to the sum of the orders of its poles, <math>\Sigma n</math>; which is briefly expressed by saying that the number of its zeros is equal to the number of its poles. Applying this theorem to the function <math>f(z)-\text{A}</math>, where <math>\text{A}</math> is an arbitrary constant, we have the result, that the function <math>f(z)</math> assumes the value <math>\text{A}</math> in one of the parallelograms as many times as it becomes infinite. Thus, by what is proved above, every conceivable complex value does arise as a value for the doubly periodic function <math>f(z)</math> in any one of its parallelograms, and in fact at least twice. The number of times it arises is called the ''order'' of the function; the result suggests a property of rational functions.

Consider further the integral <math>\int z\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}dz</math>, where <math>f'(z)=\frac{df(z)}{dz}</math>, taken round the perimeter of the primary parallelogram; the contribution to this arising from two opposite perimeter points such as <math>z</math> and <math>z+w</math> is of the form <math>-\omega\int\frac{f'(z)}{f(z)}dz</math>, which, as <math>z</math> increases from <math>z_0</math> to <math>z_0+\omega'</math>, gives, if <math>\lambda</math> denote the generalized logarithm, <math>-\omega\{\lambda[f(z_0+\omega')]-\lambda[f(z_0)]\}</math>, that is, since <math>f(z_0+\omega')=f(z_0)</math>, gives <math>2\pi i\text{N}\omega</math>, where <math>\text{N}</math> is an integer; similarly the result of the integration along the other two opposite sides is of the form <math>2\pi i\text{N}'\omega'</math>, where <math>\text{N}'</math> is an integer. The integral, however, is equal to <math>2\pi i</math> times the sum of the residues of <math>zf'(z)/f(z)</math> at the poles interior to the parallelogram. For a zero, of order <math>m</math>, of <math>f(z)</math> at <math>z=a</math>, the contribution to this sum is <math>2\pi ima</math>, for a pole of order <math>n</math> at <math>z=b</math> the contribution is <math>-2\pi inb</math>; we thus infer that <math>\Sigma ma-\Sigma nb=\text{N}\omega+\text{N}'\omega'</math>; this we express in words by saying that the sum of the values of <math>z</math> where <math>f(z)=0</math> within any parallelogram is equal to the sum of the values of <math>z</math> where <math>f(z)=\infty</math> save for integral multiples of the periods. By considering similarly the function <math>f(z)-\text{A}</math> where <math>\text{A}</math> is an arbitrary constant, we prove that each of these sums is equal to the sum of the values of <math>z</math> where the function takes the value <math>\text{A}</math> in the parallelogram.

We pass now to the construction of a function having two arbitrary periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math> of unreal ratio, which has a single pole of the second order in any one of its parallelograms.

For this consider first the network of parallelograms whose corners are the points <math>\Omega = m\omega + m'\omega'</math>, where <math>m</math>, <math>m'</math> take all positive and negative integer values; putting a small circle about each corner of this network, let <math>\text{P}</math> be a point outside all these circles; this will be interior to a parallelogram whose corners in order may be denoted by <math>z_0</math>, <math>z_0+\omega</math>, <math>z_0+\omega+\omega'</math>, <math>z_0+\omega'</math>; we shall denote <math>z_0</math>, <math>z_0+\omega</math> by <math>\text{A}_0</math>, <math>\text{B}_0</math>; this parallelogram <math>\Pi_0</math> is surrounded by eight other parallelograms, forming with <math>\Pi_0</math> a larger parallelogram <math>\Pi_1</math>, of which one side, for instance, contains the points <math>z_0-\omega-\omega'</math>, <math>z_0-\omega'</math>, <math>z_0-\omega'+\omega</math>, <math>z_0-\omega'+2\omega</math>, which we shall denote by <math>\text{A}_1</math>, <math>\text{B}_1</math>, <math>\text{C}_1</math>, <math>\text{D}_1</math>. This parallelogram <math>\Pi_1</math> is surrounded by sixteen of the original parallelograms, forming with <math>\Pi_1</math> a still larger parallelogram <math>\Pi_2</math> of which one side, for instance, contains the points <math>z_0-2\omega-2\omega'</math>, <math>z_0-\omega-2\omega'</math>, <math>z_0-2\omega'</math>, <math>z_0+\omega-2\omega'</math>, <math>z_0+2\omega-2\omega'</math>, <math>z_0+3\omega-2\omega'</math>, which we shall denote by <math>\text{A}_2</math>, <math>\text{B}_2</math>, <math>\text{C}_2</math>, <math>\text{D}_2</math>, <math>\text{E}_2</math>, <math>\text{F}_2</math>. And so on. Now consider the sum of the inverse cubes of the distances of the point <math>\text{P}</math> from the corners of all the original parallelograms. The sum will contain the terms
{{block center|<math>\text{S}_0 = \frac{1}{\text{PA}^3_0} + \left(\frac{1}{\text{PA}^3_1} + \frac{1}{\text{PB}^3_1} + \frac{1}{\text{PC}^3_1}\right) + \left(\frac{1}{\text{PA}^3_2} + \frac{1}{\text{PB}^3_2} + \dots + \frac{1}{\text{PE}^3_2}\right) + \dots</math>}}
and three other sets of terms, each infinite in number, formed in a similar way. If the perpendiculars from <math>\text{P}</math> to the sides <math>\text{A}_0\text{B}_0</math>, <math>\text{A}_1\text{B}_1\text{C}_1</math>, <math>\text{A}_2\text{B}_2\text{C}_2\text{D}_2\text{E}_2</math>, and so on, be <math>p</math>, <math>p+q</math>, <math>p+2q</math> and so on, the sum <math>\text{S}_0</math> is at most equal to
{{block center|<math>\frac{1}{p^3} + \frac{3}{(p+q)^3} + \frac{5}{(p+2q)^3} + \dots + \frac{2n+1}{(p+nq)^3} + \dots</math>}}
of which the general term is ultimately, when <math>n</math> is large, in a ratio of equality with <math>2q^{-3}n^{-2}</math>, so that the series <math>\text{S}_0</math> is convergent, as we know the sum <math>\Sigma n^{-2}</math> to be; this assumes that <math>p \neq 0</math>; if <math>\text{P}</math> be on <math>\text{A}_0\text{B}_0</math> the proof for the convergence of <math>\text{S}_0-1/\text{PA}^3_0</math> is the same. Taking the three other sums analogous to <math>\text{S}_0</math> we thus reach the result that the series {{block center|<math>\phi(z) = -2\Sigma(z-\Omega)^{-3},</math>}}
where <math>\Omega</math> is <math>m\omega+m'\omega'</math>, and <math>m</math>, <math>m'</math> are to take all positive and negative integer values, and <math>z</math> is any point outside small circles described with the points <math>\Omega</math> as centres, is ''absolutely convergent.'' Its sum is therefore independent of the order of its terms. By the nature of the proof, which holds for all positions of <math>z</math> outside the small circles spoken of, the series is also clearly ''uniformly convergent'' outside these circles. Each term of the series being a monogenic function of <math>z</math>, the series may therefore be differentiated and integrated outside these circles, and represents a monogenic function. It is clearly periodic with the periods <math>\omega</math>, <math>\omega'</math>; for <math>\phi(z+\omega)</math> is the same sum as <math>\phi(z)</math> with the terms in a slightly different order. Thus <math>\phi(z+\omega) = \phi(z)</math> and <math>\phi(z+\omega') = \phi(z)</math>.

Consider now the function
{{block center|<math>f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2}+\int_0^z \left\{ \phi(z)+\frac{2}{z^3} \right\} dz,</math>}}
where, for the subject of integration, the area of uniform convergence clearly includes the point <math>z=0</math>; this gives
{{block center|<math>\frac{df(z)}{dz} = \phi(z)</math>}}
{{block center|and <math>f(z) = \frac{1}{z^2}+\Sigma' \left\{ \frac{1}{(z-\Omega)^2}-\frac{1}{\Omega^2} \right\},</math>}}
wherein <math>\Sigma'</math> is a sum excluding the term for which <math>m=0</math> and <math>m'=0</math>. Hence <math>f(z+\omega)-f(z)</math> and <math>f(z+\omega')-f(z)</math> are both independent of <math>z</math>. Noticing, however, that, by its form, <math>f(z)</math> is an even function of <math>z</math>, and putting <math>z=-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega</math>, <math>z=-\tfrac{1}{2}\omega'</math> respectively, we infer that also <math>f(z)</math> has the two periods <math>\omega</math> and <math>\omega'</math>. In the primary parallelogram <math>\Pi_0</math>, however, <math>f(z)</math> is only infinite at <math>z=0</math> in the neighbourhood of which its expansion is of the form <math>z^{-2}+</math> (power series in <math>z</math>). Thus <math>f(z)</math> is such a doubly periodic function as was to be constructed, having in any parallelogram of periods only one pole, of the second order.

It can be shown that any single valued meromorphic function of <math>z</math> with <math>\omega</math> and <math>\omega'</math> as periods can be expressed rationally in terms of <math>f(z)</math> and <math>\phi(z)</math>, and that <math>[\phi(z)]^2</math> is of the form <math>4[f(z)]^3+\text{A}f(z)+\text{B}</math>, where <math>\text{A}</math>, <math>\text{B}</math> are constants.<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
